Build a native iOS Solitaire (Klondike) game — SwiftUI, 100% local, zero
network calls, zero sign-in/accounts/analytics/telemetry of any kind. No
backend. All state (stats, settings, saved game) persists on-device only.

THE CENTRAL CONSTRAINT — READ THIS FIRST: this must be a real, fully
playable, correctly-rules-implemented Klondike solitaire game. Drag-and-drop
(or tap-to-move) card interaction, legal-move validation, win detection,
undo, new-game/deal, and a stock/waste/foundation/tableau layout that
actually works. Do not let the visual ambition come at the cost of the game
being playable and correct — a beautiful app that can't be played is a
failure.

VISUAL DESIGN — THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST WIN AWARDS:
Cards must look like real, tactile playing cards — not the generic flat
rounded-rectangles-with-tiny-corner-pips that every solitaire clone uses.
Invent a genuinely original custom card face system: bespoke rank/suit
typography or iconography (not SF Symbols reused as suit glyphs), a
consistent illustrated or generative pattern language across all 52 cards
and the card back, real card-stock texture/shadow/lighting, and satisfying
physical motion (cards should feel like they have weight — spring-based
drag, believable flip/deal animation, subtle parallax or depth).

The bar: this should look and feel like something from an Apple Design
Award reel, not a tutorial app. Judge yourself against that bar throughout
— if a screen looks like a stock SwiftUI solitaire tutorial, it has failed
the brief. One clear, original visual "hook" (an art direction, a material
language, a signature interaction) should be identifiable in one glance
that no other solitaire app has.

Also include: light/dark mode (both fully art-directed, not just inverted
colors), haptics on card moves/wins, a stats screen (games played/won,
best time, streak — all local), and a settings screen (draw-1 vs draw-3,
card back selection, timer on/off).

Ship something that could realistically be submitted to the App Store today
and be visually distinctive in a screenshot alone.

### Round 2


**Codex (Design Lead · Systems Thinker) — Round 2**

I’m siding with Claude on the open disagreement and locking this to v1 as “no built-in social/seed sharing mechanics.” Codex, your challenge-seed idea is a good idea in a vacuum, but here it doesn’t fit the constraints cleanly: we already have explicit non-goals around social/multiplayer and no-network/offline behavior, and introducing seeded replay would force a side-channel rules path that risks violating “fresh real-RNG shuffle every new game” unless it’s a separate mode you have to design and document anyway. That is the wrong complexity budget for this phase, and it creates a credibility drag exactly where the app needs deterministic correctness guarantees. So for this build, growth is not a feature surface, it is a product property.

For users, this is a five-to-fifteen-minute reliability game for people who bounce between tasks and want to resume instantly, plus a design-forward player who judges the screenshot first before trust in the app. The concrete user promise is simple: it must always feel like it knows exactly where every card is and always recover cleanly; one wrong legal/illegal decision or one corrupt reload is a total brand failure. The value people “pay” for is not vanity: it’s the cost they avoid from ad/telemetry clutter, fake progression pressure, and bad UX that breaks confidence. In this brief, paid value is the retention value of trust plus interruption safety, not a feature unlock.

Subscription value is intentionally nil in v1. There is no paywall, no IAP, no cloud account tier, no streak monetization game layer, no “pro” unlock because DEC-prompt_contract-010 and the current app contract already close that lane. If we talk about value, it’s this: users keep opening because the app is faster, safer, more legible, and less cognitively expensive than every freemium solitaire they’ve deleted. Any future subscription idea (cloud restore, journals, solver) is a new product decision and not part of this phase.

Core loop stays exactly where it’s strongest: launch into active board or a fresh deal, drag or tap to move with instant legal/illegal feedback, draw/recycle per locked draw mode, inline multi-step undo, explicit win or stuck-board end states, and New Game with clean state reset. The loop has to stay interruption-safe: pause/resume, timer semantics per session, and persistence only from settled logical state. The local rule is: no hidden outcomes, no fake counters, no partial-state lies.

Competitive wedge is the hard one, and we should keep it defensible: award-level tactile visual identity + canonical Klondike correctness + local-first integrity with zero analytics/no network/no accounts. The app doesn’t need a social flywheel if it can survive being evaluated at arm’s length in one glance and one move. Viral or niche growth mechanism is therefore screenshot-driven reputation + word-of-mouth in design and gaming communities: people share a clean winning board, the card hook, or the deal reveal moment because it’s visually identifiable immediately. That only works if first-session motion and glyph legibility are nailed at real card size.

Local-first behavior is strict: all game, settings, and stats are on-device only, using local models with migration-safe versioning, and a visible disclosure in Settings that reinstall/device migration wipes progress because that’s the documented behavior, not a hidden trap. The cloud-ready path is a clean persistence interface: define a transport-agnostic store protocol now, keep local SwiftData/UserDefaults/FileManager as the current adapter, and leave a future encrypted, opt-in sync adapter as an adapter swap only. This keeps v1 clean, fully independent, and still prevents a rewrite if a future product decision reopens cloud or subscription features.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 2**

Let me push back on my own round-1 position because Codex's challenge-seed idea deserves a real hearing, not a dismissal — but I still land somewhere different from where Codex put it.

Codex's instinct is right that "someone screenshots it unprompted" is a passive bet, and passive bets are how growth mechanisms quietly become "we hoped." I was too conservative saying zero feature surface — if the entire growth story rests on screenshots, the app should at least make screenshotting/sharing frictionless at the exact moment someone's most likely to want to, which is the win screen. So I'm updating: some kind of native share affordance on win belongs in this brief. But the specific mechanism Codex proposed — a challenge seed that reproduces the identical deal for a friend to replay — I think is the wrong shape for what this app can actually afford to build safely, and I want to walk through why concretely rather than just asserting it.

A shareable seed only works if the shuffle is genuinely reproducible from that seed, on a different device, possibly a different iOS version, possibly a different Swift runtime. `SystemRandomNumberGenerator` is explicitly not a documented, versioned algorithm — Apple doesn't guarantee it produces the same output from the same seed across OS versions, because it's backed by the system CSPRNG, not a deterministic PRNG. So "seeded replay" as a feature actually requires standing up a second, hand-rolled deterministic RNG (something like a splitmix64 or PCG implementation) that lives entirely separately from the real-shuffle path used for every actual game. That's not a small add — it's a second RNG implementation, a second Fisher-Yates path, and now two things that both claim to produce "a valid shuffled Klondike deal" that have to be kept in sync forever, tested separately, and verified to never leak into each other. DEC-prompt_contract-011 already locks "fresh real-RNG shuffle every new game" as a correctness requirement with automated-reject teeth — the moment there are two shuffle code paths in the codebase, any verification pass has to prove the real-play path never accidentally takes the deterministic one, which is exactly the kind of subtle state-machine bug this fleet has shipped before. And per the ordering rule we all just agreed on in round 1 — correctness work is never the thing that gets cut, visual polish is — building a second RNG system to support a growth feature is spending correctness-tier engineering budget on a feature that is, honestly, unproven. Nobody knows if solitaire players actually want to compare identical deals with friends. That's a real behavioral assumption Codex is making with zero evidence behind it, in an app that already carries the ASSUMPTION tag on its entire target-audience framing per product_research.

So here's the closing call I want to make instead of leaving this open into design: kill the seed/replay mechanic, and replace it with the cheap, low-risk version of the same instinct — a one-tap native share sheet on the win screen that shares a rendered image of the completed board (the foundations, maybe with a "solved in 4:32" caption baked into the image). Zero backend, zero new RNG path, zero comparison surface, zero anything that could be read as brushing against the no-social/no-multiplayer non-goal, because there's no in-app mechanism for anyone to do anything with what they receive except look at a picture — same as any other iOS share-sheet use. It directly serves the "make the organic screenshot moment frictionless" goal without inventing new correctness surface area, and it's something a build phase can actually finish and verify (render an image, hand it to `UIActivityViewController` — that's it, no golden-seed test suite required). If a future version wants to build actual seeded challenge replay later, that's a real feature with real infrastructure cost that deserves its own scoped decision, not something we wave through here because it sounds nice in a product brief.

One more thing I want on record before this closes, reacting to the Coordinator's summary: it framed this as "does v1 ship a share feature or not," but I think the more precise framing is "does v1 ship a share feature that requires new game-logic infrastructure, or one that's pure presentation." That's the actual fork, and pure-presentation wins every time under this app's own locked doctrine. I'm calling this settled — win screen gets a share button, it shares an image, nothing else changes, and the challenge-seed idea gets explicitly logged as rejected-for-v1 so nobody quietly resurrects it mid-build thinking it was pre-approved.
